notes.b: Protein does far more in the body than most nutrients. Its jobs fall into three groups: building structures, regulating and defending the body, and supplying amino acids (the small units protein is made from).
points: Structural proteins build and maintain body tissues such as cells, muscle, skin and connective tissue, so they give the body its shape and strength.
Physiologically active proteins regulate body processes, acting as hormones, enzymes, antibodies and blood proteins, so they keep the body working and defend it.
Nutrient proteins are the proteins of food that supply amino acids, including the essential amino acids the body cannot make, so they are the raw material for the other two groups.
notes.tip: For Higher Level, use the three class headings (structural, physiologically active and nutrient) when you list functions, and give examples under each.

notes.b: Structural proteins are the building material of the body. Cells and tissues are made largely of protein, so the amino acids in food are needed to make new tissue and to mend old tissue.
points: Growth and repair: amino acids from protein are used to make new body cells, for example during childhood growth and pregnancy, and to repair damaged tissue such as a wound.
Muscle: myosin and actin filaments make up muscle fibres and contract to produce movement, which is why muscle is built from protein.
Connective tissue: collagen forms the fibres of tendons (which join muscle to bone), ligaments (which join bone to bone) and skin, giving them strength.
Hair and nails: keratin, a structural protein, forms hair and nails.
Cell membranes: proteins are built into the membranes around cells, helping to control what passes in and out.
notes.tip: Always include growth and repair when asked for functions of protein. Muscle, skin and cell membranes are structural, so do not file them under the active proteins.

notes.b: Some proteins do not build anything. They work inside the body to control reactions, fight infection and carry substances, and this is why they are called physiologically active.
points: Hormones: protein hormones such as insulin, made in the pancreas, control processes like blood glucose levels. Insulin is a hormone, not an enzyme.
Enzymes: protein catalysts (substances that speed up a reaction without being used up) speed up chemical reactions, for example pepsin, which breaks down protein in the stomach.
Antibodies: proteins made by white blood cells bind to invading micro-organisms and toxins as part of the immune response, so they help the body fight infection.
Blood plasma proteins: albumin keeps water within the blood vessels, helping to maintain blood volume and pressure.
Clotting proteins: fibrinogen is converted to fibrin, which forms the mesh that stops bleeding after an injury.
Haemoglobin, a protein in red blood cells, carries oxygen from the lungs to the body tissues.
Nucleoproteins are proteins combined with nucleic acid, found in chromosomes, and are listed as physiologically active proteins.
notes.tip: Hormones, enzymes and antibodies are active, not structural, so do not file enzymes as structural. Give a named example for each of hormone (insulin), enzyme (pepsin) and antibody. Nucleoproteins are listed as a physiologically active protein in the Higher Level three-class question.

notes.b: Nutrient protein means the protein in the food we eat, seen as a source of amino acids. The body digests it and rebuilds the amino acids into its own proteins.
points: Nutrient proteins supply the essential amino acids that the body cannot manufacture and must obtain from food.
Amino acids supplied by food are used to make the body's own structural and active proteins, so food protein ends up as muscle, enzymes, hormones and so on.
Surplus amino acids are not stored as protein and can be used for energy. There is more on this in Energy value.
notes.tip: Energy is a secondary use of protein, when carbohydrate and fat are short, so do not make it the main function. Nutrient protein is protein as food, not a protein doing a nutrient job inside cells.

notes.h: The three classes at a glance
notes.b: A common exam layout sets the three classes against their functions, with an example of each. It is a quick way to learn the whole topic.
points: Structural: growth and repair of body cells, muscles and skin. Examples: collagen in skin and tendons, keratin in hair and nails.
Physiologically active: hormones, enzymes, antibodies, blood proteins and nucleoproteins. Examples: insulin, pepsin, albumin, haemoglobin.
Nutrient: provide the essential amino acids the body cannot make, with excess protein used for energy. The example is the protein in food.
notes.tip: A table of the three groups and their functions is asked at Higher Level: structural covers growth and repair of cells, muscles and skin, active covers hormones, enzymes, antibodies, blood proteins and nucleoproteins, and nutrient covers essential amino acids and excess for energy.

keyTerms.definition: A protein that builds and maintains body tissues, such as collagen in connective tissue or myosin in muscle.
A protein that regulates body processes, such as a hormone, enzyme, antibody or blood plasma protein.
A protein in food that supplies amino acids, including the essential amino acids the body cannot make.
A protein that acts as a biological catalyst, speeding up a specific chemical reaction in the body.
A chemical messenger made by a gland and carried in the blood to control a process in another part of the body.
A protein made by white blood cells that binds to a specific invading micro-organism or toxin to help destroy it.
A fibrous structural protein that forms connective tissue, tendons, ligaments and skin, giving them strength.
A protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to the body's tissues.
A protein dissolved in the liquid part of the blood, such as albumin or fibrinogen, that has a role in blood volume or clotting.

questions.prompt: Outline two functions of protein that help to build or maintain body tissue, and name one protein that carries out each function.
questions.model: Growth and repair of body cells, using amino acids to make new cells and repair damaged tissue, for example collagen in connective tissue. Formation of muscle, with myosin and actin contracting to produce movement. Keratin forms hair and nails, and collagen gives skin and tendons strength.

questions.prompt: Describe the three biological functions of protein in the body, giving at least one named protein or example for each function.
questions.model: Structural proteins build and maintain body tissues: growth and repair of cells, formation of muscle with myosin and actin, collagen in connective tissue and skin, keratin in hair and nails, and proteins in cell membranes. Physiologically active proteins regulate body processes: hormones such as insulin control blood glucose; enzymes such as pepsin speed up digestion in the stomach; antibodies produced by white blood cells fight invading micro-organisms and toxins; albumin maintains blood volume and fibrinogen helps the blood clot; haemoglobin carries oxygen in red blood cells. Nutrient proteins supply the essential amino acids that the body cannot make, and surplus amino acids are used for energy.
